slides.title: What do you remember from yesterday?
bullets: Can you name the three states of matter?
How are the particles arranged differently in a solid, a liquid and a gas?
What happens to particles when they are given more energy?

slides.title: What happens when wax is heated?
bullets: Solid wax has tightly packed particles in a fixed arrangement — it keeps its shape.
When heated, the particles gain energy and begin to move — the wax melts into a liquid.
This change of state from solid to liquid is called MELTING.

slides.title: What happens to particles when heated further?
bullets: At 0°C, ice melts into liquid water — particles slide past each other.
At 100°C, liquid water boils and becomes water vapour — particles escape into the air.
Boiling and evaporating both turn a liquid into a gas, but at different rates.

slides.title: Is the white cloud above the kettle steam?
bullets: Steam is water in gas form — it is completely invisible.
The white cloud you can see is actually tiny droplets of liquid water that have already condensed from the hot steam.
Misconception: the white cloud is NOT steam — steam is the invisible gas just above the spout.

slides.title: Annotate the heating diagram
bullets: On your LP, label the three states of matter on the heating diagram.
Add the temperature labels: 0°C and 100°C at the correct change points.
Write the correct process name for each arrow: melting, boiling or evaporating.
Challenge: add a fourth arrow going the other way — what process does it show?

sections.text: When ice (solid) is heated to 0°C, the particles gain energy and begin to move. They slide past each other and the ice melts into liquid water. When heated further to 100°C the particles move so fast they escape into the air as a gas (water vapour). The particles are furthest apart in the gas state.
Arrow labels: MELTING (solid to liquid, 0°C)   BOILING / EVAPORATING (liquid to gas, 100°C)
